title: Container Apps vs AKS
description: Compare Azure Container Apps and AKS to understand when to use each platform for containerized workloads.

data.text: Both Container Apps and AKS run containers on Azure, but they serve different audiences. Container Apps abstracts Kubernetes entirely, while AKS exposes the full Kubernetes API.

cards.title: Container Apps
cards.description: Serverless container platform built on Kubernetes.

cards.title: AKS
cards.description: Managed Kubernetes cluster with full API access.

rows: Scale to zero to save costs

data.title: Start with Container Apps
data.text: If you are unsure, start with Container Apps. It offers the simplest path to production. You can migrate to AKS later if you need deeper Kubernetes control.

data.caption: Decision tree for choosing a container platform
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    Q1{Need Kubernetes API?} -->|No| CA[Container Apps]
    Q1 -->|Yes| Q2{Have K8s expertise?}
    Q2 -->|Yes| AKS[AKS]
    Q2 -->|No| Q3{Can you learn K8s?}
    Q3 -->|Yes| AKS
    Q3 -->|No| CA

data.text: Deploy the Same Container Two Ways
Container Apps takes an image and a few flags; AKS takes a cluster plus Kubernetes manifests. The difference in ceremony is the point of the comparison.

data.title: Container Apps: one command from source to URL
data.content: `az containerapp up` builds the image, pushes it, creates the environment, and deploys the app. The ingress endpoint is returned at the end.
data.code:
az containerapp up \
  --name demo-api \
  --resource-group rg-demo \
  --location westeurope \
  --source . \
  --target-port 8080 \
  --ingress external

data.title: AKS: a Deployment and a Service
data.content: The cluster must already exist. Kubernetes schedules the pods, and the LoadBalancer service provisions an Azure load balancer.
data.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: demo-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: demo-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: demo-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: demo-api
          image: myregistry.azurecr.io/demo-api:1.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 256Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: demo-api
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: demo-api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

data.title: Apply the manifests and check the rollout
data.content: `kubectl apply` is declarative: running it repeatedly converges the cluster to the file. `kubectl rollout status` blocks until the new pods are ready.
data.code:
az aks get-credentials \
  --resource-group rg-demo \
  --name aks-demo

kubectl apply -f demo-api.yaml
kubectl rollout status deployment/demo-api
kubectl get pods,svc -l app=demo-api

data.title: Interview angle: what you give up with Container Apps
data.text: Container Apps gives you scaling, revisions, ingress, and Dapr without exposing the Kubernetes API. You give up custom controllers, CRDs, node-pool tuning, privileged pods, and full control of the cluster network. If the team's requirement is 'run this container and scale it', Container Apps is usually enough. If the requirement is 'we need the Kubernetes API for operators or platform tooling', that is when AKS becomes the honest answer.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Container Apps: serverless, abstracts Kubernetes, simpler
AKS: full Kubernetes control, more operational responsibility
Choose Container Apps for simplicity and cost savings
Choose AKS for full Kubernetes feature access
data.takeaway: Pick the platform that matches your team's expertise and operational needs.
